- Title: Influence of the Spatial and Temporal Interaction Between Diesel Pilot and Directly Injected Natural Gas Jet on Ignition and Combustion Characteristics
- Paper ID / source record: A007 / A-NG-07
- Original PDF: `02_PDF_Raw/A/A-NG-07_2018_Fink_DieselPilot_NGJet_SpatialTemporalInteraction.pdf`
Primary Tier 1 chronology and interaction pillar for pilot-ignited HPDI natural-gas combustion.
How do relative injection timing and jet angle jointly control pilot ignition, transfer to the gas jet, and heat-release shape?
Primary RCEM experiment with separate single-hole injectors, shadowgraphy, pressure/position measurements, and a multizone heat-loss model for HRR.
200 mm bore, 14 dm3 RCEM; jet angle varied from -90 to +30 deg; injector origins offset by about 5 mm.
TDC 75 +/- 1.5 bar and 780 +/- 4 K. Diesel: 2000 bar, 3 mg, 395 us, SOI -2 ms ATDC. Gas: 330 bar, 80 mg, 2730 us; gas SOI -2.5 to +1.5 ms relative to pilot.
No underexpanded-jet shock topology is quantified; shadowgraphy resolves jet/spray overlap and density-gradient structures.
Diesel pilot and natural-gas jet; no droplet-size distribution is reported.
No comparison-ready NPR, We, Re, Oh, or Mach value is reported; pressure bases are not assumed.
Pilot and gas SOI, ignition thresholds, and SOI separation are typed. HRR history is figure-only and not digitized.
Strong interaction can delay or prevent pilot ignition, but proper overlap promotes gas ignition. Gas-ignition timing relative to SOI organizes HRR shape.
Ignition becomes possible below about +25 deg between diverging jets; tested timing/angle ranges and injection conditions are retained.

Authors attribute pilot deterioration to gas-driven dilution or isolation from air entrainment, local cooling, and possibly altered kinetics; gas ignition benefits from contact with burned pilot products.
Timing and angle set overlap -> overlap modifies pilot mixture/ignition -> burned pilot region ignites gas -> ignition relative to gas SOI sets premixing -> premixing shapes HRR.
The pilot/gas ignition trade-off constrains combustion stability and controllable premixing; +10 to +20 deg is proposed as a robust compromise.
Table 1 p.2; ignition definitions Fig. 6 p.4; operability Figs. 7-9 p.5; gas delay Fig. 10 p.6; HRR Figs. 11-12 pp.6-7; conclusions pp.7-8.
Operating values and qualitative boundaries are reported. HRR is pressure-model derived. No external property lookup or figure digitization was used.
RCEM lacks swirl, walls and adjacent jets of an engine; hot-product heat losses are neglected, so HRR supports qualitative comparisons rather than burnout completeness.
T1-A007-C01 to C03 retain the ignition trade-off, HRR timing descriptor, and geometry design implication.
Compare with other HPDI timing papers only after matching injection-sequence definitions, angle convention, operating state, and ignition metric.
None. Schema 1.1 represents chronology, intervals, interaction geometry, and process relations.
Provides a source-localized pilot -> gas ignition -> combustion chronology for the review mainline.

- Title: Numerical characterization of hydrogen under-expanded jets with a focus on Internal Combustion Engines applications
- Paper ID / source record: B021 / B-E-01
- Original PDF: `02_PDF_Raw/B/B-E-01_2023_Anaclerio_Numerical_Underexpanded_HydrogenJets_ICE.pdf`
Tier 1 gas-dynamic anchor for contextual NPR, Mach-disk scaling, ICE transients, thermal diffusion, and multi-hole interaction.
How do NPR, ICE pressure/temperature histories, and jet spacing control hydrogen shock topology and mixing?
Steady/unsteady RANS with ideal and cubic real-gas EoS tests; axisymmetric single jet plus 3D parallel multi-jet cases.
Convergent 1 mm nozzle for NPR sweep; ICE case uses 0.61 mm holes; multi-jet cases use 1 or 2 mm inter-axis spacing.
NPR is total plenum/upstream pressure divided by discharge/chamber static pressure. Sweep 2.5-60; ICE upstream 100 bar with chamber 6.15-32.94 bar.
Moderate NPR gives diamond cells; higher NPR gives Mach reflection and Mach disk; very high NPR is first-cell dominated.
NA: gas-only study; no liquid droplet or spray breakup.
NPR is contextually linked. Froude values are reported for buoyancy assessment but are not generalized beyond the modeled setup.
ICE injection lasts 4.9 ms; NPR decreases from 16.24 to 2.97. NPR and Mach-disk histories are registered without curve digitization.
NPR increases near-field dimensions; temperature affects H2 diffusion rather than Mach-disk position; 1 mm inter-axis jets bend together whereas 2 mm cases do not.
Tables 2-6 provide Mach-disk dimensions, error comparisons, and ICE states; selected endpoints and context are promoted to the master table.
Pressure-ratio-driven expansion establishes shock structure; Soret-enabled thermal diffusion affects far-field mixing; inter-jet expansion waves create a low-pressure attraction region.
NPR -> expansion/shock topology -> local velocity field -> H2 transport; spacing -> inter-jet wave field -> low pressure -> deflection/coalescence.
Near-field resolution affects predicted mixture formation; temperature and multi-jet interaction alter hydrogen distribution relevant to ICE combustion.
Boundary conditions p.4; EoS Fig.10 p.7; NPR Eqs.7-9/Tables2-3 pp.7-9; ICE Fig.16/Tables4-6 pp.9-10; hysteresis pp.11-12; temperature p.12; multi-jet pp.13-15.

- Title: Numerical study of the transcritical shock-droplet interaction
- Paper ID / source record: C029 / C-PC-03
- Original PDF: `02_PDF_Raw/C/C-PC-03_2021_Boyd_Transcritical_ShockDroplet_Interaction.pdf`
Tier 1 transcritical shock-droplet pillar bridging classical liquid SDI and gas-bubble SBI behavior.
How do thermodynamic state, pressure and incident Mach control shock refraction, vorticity, deformation and breakup near the Widom line?
2D axisymmetric inviscid diffuse-interface simulation with a modified Peng-Robinson EoS and hybrid conservative/double-flux solver.
5 cm n-dodecane droplet in nitrogen; domain and grid are reported; temperature, pressure and Mach are varied independently.
Preshock temperature 500-800 K, pressure 2-10 MPa, incident shock Mach 1.2-2.0. Pressure basis is thermodynamic but not relabeled absolute/gauge.
SoS ratio n=cS/cD governs diverging/converging refraction; positive impedance mismatch persists, distinguishing TSDI from classic SBI.
n-dodecane initially spans liquidlike to gaslike supercritical states; surface tension is neglected in the solver and approximated only for a Weber estimate.
Incident Mach is laboratory-frame shock Mach. We uses postshock density/velocity, D0 and approximate sigma. Named SoS ratios use explicit operands.
Shock impact starts t=0; breakup time t* is normalized by postshock velocity, D0 and density ratio. Circulation histories are figure-only.
n=1 separates diverging and converging behavior; strong convergence creates focal pressure/axial jetting; Mach changes circulation and morphology.
Tables I-III report temperature, pressure and Mach case states. Selected components and thresholds are atomized with exact source locators.
Widom-line state change modifies SoS ratio; shock convergence establishes focal pressure; baroclinic deposition seeds vorticity and interfacial instability.
Thermodynamic state -> refraction/convergence -> pressure/vorticity field -> interface instability and droplet deformation.
The paper links early transcritical breakup/mixing physics to high-pressure propulsion, but does not model ignition or combustion.
Transcritical definition pp.2-3; method pp.3-5; critical ratios pp.5-7; setup pp.7-10; temperature pp.11-20; pressure pp.21-25; Mach pp.25-30; Tables I-III pp.31-32.
All retained values are source-reported. The approximate Weber number is labeled as author-reported approximation; no external fluid properties were added.
Inviscid 2D axisymmetric early-time model; no surface tension/diffusion/thermal conduction/chemistry; late 3D breakup not resolved.
T1-C029-C01 to C03 retain state/topology, convergence/jetting, and shock-strength/morphology evidence.
Compare with classical SDI/SBI only after matching SoS ratio, impedance, density ratio, pressure, temperature and Mach definitions.
None blocking. Generic ratios and source-limited component definitions fit Schema 1.1.
Provides the thermodynamic-state bridge between shock structure and droplet response.

- Title: Comparative analysis of detonation and shock waves interacting with droplets: Characteristics and mechanisms
- Paper ID / source record: D019 / D-DW-04
- Original PDF: `02_PDF_Raw/D/D-DW-04_2026_Zou_DetonationShock_DropletInteraction_Mechanisms.pdf`
Tier 1 comparative application evidence for reaction-heat-release effects on wave, cavitation and breakup mechanisms.
How do equal-leading-strength detonation and inert shock waves differ in reflected waves, cavitation timescales and droplet deformation?
2D multicomponent compressible two-phase simulation with chemical-potential phase transition and two-step detonation chemistry.
Planar wave impacting a 4.8 mm water droplet; 5 um grid selected; 2D configuration is treated as an upper-bound estimate of interaction intensity.
Stoichiometric H2/O2 with 70% Ar at 300 K and 50 kPa; inert shock modeled as zero-reaction detonation with equal leading-shock Mach 4.8.
Early topology is similar, but postwave pressure/temperature/velocity states change reflected-shock propagation and low-pressure persistence.
Water droplet. Phase transition is enabled for cavitation analysis and disabled only for uncluttered wave-topology comparison.
Reported We/Re differ strongly between detonation and shock cases; source does not atomize all component definitions, so NV components are retained.
Thermal conduction O(1e2 s) versus deformation O(1e-4 s) motivates omission for the main droplet; vapor history is figure-only.
Detonation accelerates reflected shocks, shortens/asymmetrizes cavitation collapse, and produces leeward flattening rather than shock-case RT forward jetting.
Table I gives We/Re; mesh and timescale values are localized; no figure values were digitized.
Reaction heat release changes postwave sound speed and velocity; pressure attenuation shortens low-pressure duration; postwave velocity controls recirculation and RT response.
Wave type/heat release -> postwave state -> reflected/expansion wave loading -> cavitation and vortex/instability response -> deformation/breakup.
Application relevance is to detonation propulsion; transfer to HPDI/shock-droplet review is comparative agent synthesis, not an author claim about engines.
Setup/Table I pp.3-4; method pp.4-7; mesh pp.7-8; wave comparison pp.10-15; cavitation pp.16-20; deformation pp.20-24; conclusions p.24.
